items.originalTitle: Opus 5.5 agents discover two room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates
items.summary:
A team using Opus 5.5 AI agents has discovered two candidate materials for room-temperature magnetic semiconductors, which could advance spintronics technology by enabling efficient spin sorting without macroscopic magnetic fields. One candidate was designed by the AI agents, while the other was first synthesized in 1999 and predicted by their calculations to have the desired properties.

The research focuses on materials that combine features of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, aiming for a type called Luttinger compensated magnets that allow spin sorting by energy without generating external magnetic fields. This could improve data storage technologies by enabling faster, more compact, and energy-efficient spintronic devices.

items.originalTitle: Beam: Reflection's 501B open-weight model
items.summary:
Reflection has launched Beam, its first open-weight model featuring 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters, designed for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. The model was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens from diverse, high-quality datasets and underwent extensive reinforcement learning using 10,500 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs over four weeks, generating over 100 million rollouts to enhance its capabilities and inference efficiency.

Beam demonstrates competitive performance with larger open models like GLM 5.2 and Qwen 3.8-Max, particularly excelling in inference compute efficiency, making it suitable for enterprise coding and agentic applications. The model incorporates innovations in asynchronous policy gradient reinforcement learning to maintain stability at scale and offers users control over reasoning effort to balance performance and token usage. Beam is currently in final evaluation stages, with plans to release its weights, technical report, and developer tools later this month.

items.originalTitle: ChatGPT is adding real cartoonists' signatures to fake New Yorker cartoons
items.summary:
OpenAI's ChatGPT has been generating AI-created cartoons in the style of The New Yorker and falsely attributing them to real cartoonists by reproducing their signatures without consent. Cartoonists like Brendan Loper have reported seeing their pen names used on AI-generated images they did not create, raising concerns about personal and creative rights violations.

The issue surfaced after viral AI-generated cartoons appeared on social media, signed with names of prominent New Yorker contributors. OpenAI acknowledged the problem and updated ChatGPT to warn users about prompts that may violate content similarity rules, but the chatbot still occasionally outputs cartoons signed with real artists' names. This practice highlights ongoing challenges around AI-generated content, attribution, and intellectual property in creative fields.

These gains are similar to those from Khan Academy practice without AI assistance. The study noted that while 96 percent of students tried Khanmigo, engagement was limited, with most interactions being brief and infrequent. The researchers suggest that increasing student engagement is critical to realizing the full potential of AI tutoring in education.

Android Authority also found evidence of granular permission settings for Gemini's actions within individual apps, which could let users control which apps Gemini can access and opt out of receiving automated calls. However, it remains uncertain whether Google will publicly release this expanded functionality or the detailed permission controls.

items.originalTitle: Our approach to EU text provenance rules
items.summary:
OpenAI is implementing text watermarking for certain models in the European Union to comply with the EU AI Act's requirements for machine-readable identification of AI-generated text. The watermarking, called textGrain, adds an invisible statistical signal to model outputs, and detection access will initially be limited to approved researchers and expert organizations to evaluate and improve the technology.

The watermarking will be optional for API customers globally and will be enabled by default for eligible ChatGPT and Codex outputs in the EU. OpenAI acknowledges limitations in detection accuracy, especially for shorter or heavily edited texts, and plans to release technical details and open-source tools to support transparency and further development. Verification tools for AI-generated images and audio will remain publicly accessible.

items.title: Researchers find vulnerabilities in Model Context Protocol enabling malicious prompt injection across AI agents at Google, Rapid7, and others [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MCP for agent-to-agent comms may be the riskiest protocol you've never heard of
items.summary:
Security researchers have identified a structural flaw in the Model Context Protocol (MCP), used for communication between AI agents, that allows attackers to spread malicious prompts from one agent to others within a network. This vulnerability, found in agents from Google, Rapid7, and several other organizations, exploits trust assumptions between agents, enabling harmful instructions to propagate and potentially cause unauthorized actions such as data exfiltration or server-side request forgery.

The flaw arises because MCP servers store credentials and agents inherently trust each other, lacking sufficient guardrails to prevent malicious prompt injection. Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin demonstrated proof-of-concept attacks exploiting this trust gap, which he terms "protocol pivoting," where an attacker leverages one protocol to escalate privileges via another. Google addressed a severe vulnerability by implementing IP allow-lists and block lists, while Rapid7 fixed a lower-severity issue. Experts warn that MCP's rapid adoption without thorough security hardening poses ongoing risks, especially as organizations build complex AI agent architectures without zero-trust principles.

OpenAI announced it will begin embedding an invisible watermark in text generated by ChatGPT and Codex for users in the European Union to meet the EU AI Act's transparency requirements. The watermark subtly influences word choices to create a detectable pattern without altering model performance and travels with the text when copied. Developers worldwide can enable watermarking via API for select models, but it is not enabled globally by default.

The watermarking method, called textGrain, was developed with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale and uses a secret key to detect AI-generated content. OpenAI noted that editing, such as replacing words with synonyms, can reduce detection accuracy, and short or translated texts are harder to identify. The company cautioned that absence of a watermark does not prove human authorship, as text could be heavily edited or generated by other AI systems. This move follows similar watermarking efforts by other AI companies to comply with EU regulations.

items.title: What’s Wrong With AI Safety Testing, and How to Fix It [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What’s Wrong With AI Safety Testing, and How to Fix It
items.summary:
The idea that Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies could “embed” researchers from outside safety groups into their operations has been all the rage in recent weeks. But the devil is in the details.

AI safety researchers worry that embedded evaluators won’t have the access they need to provide meaningful oversight.

“I've become very cynical over the last three years” from “repeatedly seeing how people promise stuff and then don’t follow up on it,” said Marius Hobbhahn, CEO of Apollo Research, which has evaluated the safety of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and other companies.

Outside evaluators who report on the dangerous capabilities and unwanted behaviors of new AI models have become crucial in recent years, but their findings are only as good as their access. AI companies can withhold relevant information from the evaluators or redact their public findings. For example, an AI company could hypothetically tell an evaluator, “Well, we gave you all the access you asked for,” but meanwhile used a second cluster of AI chips the evaluator didn’t know about, said Hobbhahn.

items.originalTitle: Learning Jazz Pianist Style with Cross-Attention Conditioning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.02918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Jazz pianists develop distinctive traits that experienced listeners can often identify within seconds, yet the features underlying this recognition resist formal description. We study jazz pianist style through the lens of a pretrained symbolic music transformer, showing that its learned representations already encode pianist identity well enough for highly accurate classification across two benchmarks. We then augment the transformer with cross-attention over learned pianist identity embeddings, enabling it to generate music conditioned on a specific artist's style. Two evaluation protocols confirm that the generator captures meaningful stylistic structure: a sliding-window classifier consistently attributes conditioned continuations to the correct artist, far above unconditioned baselines; and a classifier trained entirely on synthetic generations identifies real pianists across 12 classes with 87% chunk-level and 95% song-level accuracy. Finally, we repurpose the classifier to locate the most characteristic moments within a performance, surfacing the specific musical gestures that distinguish each pianist's voice.
